sentiment.instructions: Judge the overall sentiment the author expresses in this short social-media post. Focus on the author's own attitude or feeling (approval, excitement, gratitude, hope vs. annoyance, disappointment, criticism, fear), not merely the topic. Sarcasm counts by its intended meaning.

positive.description: The author conveys a favorable attitude: enjoyment, excitement, anticipation, praise, gratitude, love, blessing, hope, pride, or enthusiastic promotion of an event or product. Mild or partial positivity, even with a small complaint or joking tone, still counts if the overall feel is upbeat.
examples: Not even 20 pages into Paper Towns and the book centers around the night of May 5th. I know its gonna be a good one now!

neutral.description: The text mainly reports facts, news, announcements, schedules, questions, job ads, or observations without a clear emotional stance, or the feeling is ambiguous, mixed, ironic without clear direction, or too slight to call either way. Light humor or casual remarks without real approval or disapproval belong here.
examples: I may be sleep deprived but I promise you that some kid at Dunkin today looked like a sprout.

negative.description: The author conveys an unfavorable attitude: frustration, annoyance, disappointment, sadness, fear, anger, insults, mockery, criticism of people or things, complaints, or wishing harm. Also news framed around harm, danger, or trouble, and sarcastic remarks meant as criticism.
examples: The tragedy of only thinking up hilarious tweets for the Summer Olympics now is that in four years there may be no place for them.
